questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient was diagnosed with pulmonary aspergillosis. The patient was a kidney transplant patient on the immunosuppressive regimen of tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. Other medications included amlodipine. The patient was started on voriconazole 200 mg by mouth twice daily. One week later, the voriconazole trough serum concentration was 3.1 μg/mL, and the patient reported a “sunburn” despite being indoors most of the last week.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Change to anidulafungin 100 mg by mouth once daily
Change to fluconazole 400 mg by mouth once daily
Change to posaconazole DR tablets 300 mg once daily
Continue voriconazole 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Decrease voriconazole to 200 mg once daily

questions.explanation: Change to posaconazole DR tablets 300 mg once daily Voriconazole is the only azole known to carry the risk of photosensitivity reactions, including an association with skin cancers. Voriconazole is at steady state after 1 week of therapy, and the timing of the level (trough) is appropriate. The level is therapeutic (between 2 and 5.5 μg/mL). However, the adverse drug reaction is most likely attributed to voriconazole, and with other available treatment options, it would be best to use another agent. Continuing the voriconazole as is and decreasing the voriconazole are not the best options. Fluconazole does not have activity against Aspergillus. While echinocandins have activity against Aspergillus, anidulafungin monotherapy is inappropriate. Changing voriconazole to posaconazole is the most appropriate option.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q7

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient was diagnosed with disseminated histoplasmosis. The patient was known to have HIV , well controlled on cobicistat/darunavir 150/800 mg and tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine 25/200 mg by mouth once daily. The patient did not take any other medications. Kidney and liver function were normal. The patient weighed 60 kg and had no known allergies.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication regimen for empiric maintenance therapy for disseminated histoplasmosis?

options.text: Itraconazole capsules 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Itraconazole capsules 400 mg by mouth once daily
Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth once daily
Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth twice daily
Liposomal amphotericin B 300 mg IV once daily

questions.explanation: Itraconazole oral solution 200 mg by mouth once daily Itraconazole is the recommended treatment of disseminated histoplasmosis during the maintenance phase of therapy. The itraconazole oral solution formulation is preferred over the capsule formulation due to increased bioavailability. Itraconazole doses greater than 200 mg should be split into multiple doses to help optimize absorption. Itraconazole is a major substrate of CYP450 3A4. Cobicistat/darunavir is a strong CYP450 3A4 inhibitor, which will decrease the metabolism of itraconazole, resulting in increased itraconazole levels. Itraconazole inhibits the metabolism of cobicistat/darunavir, resulting in an increase in darunavir. The interaction is clinically significant. The usual, i.e., in the setting of no drug–drug interactions, itraconazole maintenance dose is 200 mg by mouth twice daily. With these drug–drug interactions in place, the recommendation is to reduce the itraconazole dose to 200 mg once daily, and then check itraconazole levels.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q6

questions.question: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole

parts.text: Explain the resistance mechanism of Candida to fluconazole

questions.model_answer: Candida resistance to fluconazole occurs via: (1) Point mutations in ERG11 (encoding lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, the azole target) that reduce drug binding affinity. (2) Overexpression/upregulation of ERG11, increasing target enzyme quantity. (3) Upregulation of efflux pumps - ABC transporters (CDR1, CDR2) and major facilitator superfamily transporters (MDR1) - that actively pump the drug out of the cell. (4) Alterations in the ergosterol biosynthetic pathway allowing bypass of the blocked step.

questions.question: Name the molecular target of each antifungal drug in the table.

parts.text: Posaconazole
Micafungin
Amphotericin
Terbinafine

questions.model_answer:
Posaconazole: lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (fungal CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis.
Micafungin: (1,3)-beta-D-glucan synthase, blocking fungal cell wall glucan synthesis.
Amphotericin B: binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that disrupt membrane integrity.
Terbinafine: squalene epoxidase, blocking an earlier step of ergosterol synthesis.

questions.question: What are 3 indications for prophylaxis with Posaconazole in clinical trials that have shown decreased mortality?

parts.text: 3 indications for Posaconazole prophylaxis showing decreased mortality

cohort_answer.text: Prevention of invasive fungal infection, lower mortality in patients with prolonged neutropenia from AML; MDS; Prevention of death as antifungal prophylaxis for GVHD. 1. Posaconazole was superior to fluconazole or itraconazole in prevention of proven or probable invasive fungal infection and resulted in lower mortality from any cause and longer survival free from proven or probable invasive fungal infection (patients with or anticipated to have neutropenia, ANC <=500 cells/mm3 for >=7 days, from remission-induction chemotherapy for newly diagnosed or first relapse AML or MDS) - Cornely et al., NEJM 2007;356(4):348-359. 2. Posaconazole was similar to fluconazole for prophylaxis against fungal infections among patients with GVHD; superior in preventing invasive aspergillosis and reducing deaths related to fungal infections (patients with GVHD receiving immunosuppressive therapy) - Ullmann et al., NEJM 2007;356(4):335-347.

parts.text: a) What is the MOA?
b) What are 2 resistance mechanisms to Fluconazole?

cohort_answer.text: a) Interacts with 14-demethylase (CYP450 enzyme converting lanosterol to ergosterol), inhibiting ergosterol synthesis and increasing cellular permeability. b) Overexpression of genes encoding lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase (ERG11, e.g. C. krusei); alterations in binding site (drug modification); drug efflux (e.g. C. glabrata). c) C. krusei and C. auris (changes in ERG11); C. norvegensis; C. inconspicua; Fusarium (possible CYP51 overexpression); Mucormycosis and Aspergillus (intrinsically resistant, mutation in CYP51); ERG11 encodes lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase, the azole target.

parts.text: I would pick _____ over _____ because patient on carbamazepine
I would pick _____ over _____ because patient has G6PD deficiency
I would pick _____ over _____ because drug NOT used for C.diff treatment and NOT associated with development of C.diff
I would pick _____ over _____ because it has superior renal penetration
I would pick _____ over _____ because it works better for CMV
I would pick _____ over _____ because I need CNS coverage

questions.model_answer:
a) Because patient is on carbamazepine (a potent CYP3A4 inducer with significant drug-interaction potential with azoles): choose caspofungin over fluconazole to avoid a clinically significant CYP-mediated interaction.
b) Because patient has G6PD deficiency: choose atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; atovaquone does not).
c) Because the drug is NOT used for C. difficile treatment and NOT associated with causing C. difficile: choose doxycycline over Septra (TMP-SMX) - doxycycline carries a low risk of precipitating C. difficile infection and is not a CDI treatment.
d) Because of superior renal/urinary penetration: choose cefazolin over cloxacillin (cefazolin achieves higher urinary concentrations; cloxacillin has substantial hepatobiliary elimination).
e) Because it works better for CMV: choose valganciclovir over acyclovir (acyclovir has minimal activity against CMV; valganciclovir/ganciclovir are the drugs of choice).
f) Because CNS coverage is needed: choose moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (moxifloxacin achieves higher CNS penetration due to greater lipophilicity).

questions.question: You see a patient with invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. Their past medical history is significant for coronary artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance of 35 mL/min).

parts.text: Based on the product monograph, the oral formulation of voriconazole is preferred to the IV formulation due to which of the patient’s comorbidities, and why?
With regard to monitoring voriconazole level, what is the minimum number of days after which the level should be checked?
What is the target voriconazole level for toxicity and effectiveness?

questions.model_answer:
a) Chronic kidney disease (CrCl 35 mL/min, <50 mL/min) - the IV voriconazole formulation is solubilized in sulfobutylether-beta-cyclodextrin (SBECD), which is renally cleared and accumulates in renal impairment (CrCl <50 mL/min); the product monograph therefore recommends the oral formulation (which does not contain this vehicle) in patients with significant renal dysfunction.
b) A trough level should be checked no sooner than after 5 days of therapy (to allow steady state, given voriconazole's nonlinear pharmacokinetics).
c) Target trough level: approximately 1-5.5 mcg/mL is considered therapeutic/effective; levels above approximately 5.5-6 mcg/mL are associated with increased toxicity (e.g., neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity).
questions.beyond_mandell: Voriconazole product monograph and therapeutic drug monitoring literature.

questions.question: Regarding azoles:

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action for azoles?
List the THREE most common mechanisms of resistance.

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action: azoles inhibit the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (encoded by ERG11), blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol; this depletes ergosterol and causes accumulation of toxic methylated sterol intermediates, disrupting fungal cell membrane structure and function.
b) Three most common resistance mechanisms: (1) Mutations in ERG11 reducing target binding affinity. (2) Overexpression/upregulation of ERG11 (target overexpression). (3) Upregulation of efflux pump expression (ABC transporters CDR1/CDR2, or major facilitator transporter MDR1).

questions.question: Q15 (2017 PM) Antifungals. Target site for: Posaconazole, Caspofungin, Terbinafine, Amphotericin

parts.text: State target site for each antifungal

cohort_answer.text: Posaconazole - lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase (inhibits conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, increased membrane permeability, cell lysis). Caspofungin - beta-(1,3)-glucan synthase (blocks glucan cross-linking of fungal cell wall, loss of osmotic resistance, cell lysis; good vs Candida biofilms). Terbinafine - squalene epoxidase (inhibits ergosterol synthesis, causes toxic squalene accumulation). Amphotericin - ergosterol (binds ergosterol, forms pores, leakage of cellular components; lower concentrations increase K+ channel activity, higher concentrations form pores).

parts.text: a) What drug class?
b) Mechanism of action
c) Activity against various fungi: Candida; Aspergillus; Dematiaceous molds (eg Mycetoma); Dimorphics; Zygomycetes (eg Mucor); Fusarium

cohort_answer.text: a) Triazoles. b) Inhibits 14-alpha lanosterol demethylase, reduces ergosterol synthesis, inhibits fungal cell membrane formation. c) Candida - yes; Aspergillus - yes; Dematiaceous molds - yes; Dimorphics - yes; Zygomycetes - no; Fusarium - yes (also Scedosporium apiospermum). d) Most common: Hepatotoxicity; QTc prolongation. Less common: visual changes/photopsia/photophobia/color change, neurotoxicity (visual hallucinations at higher conc), periostitis from fluoride excess (bone pain, high ALP), alopecia, nail changes.

b) 2 adverse effects

cohort_answer.text: a) Inhibits 14-alpha lanosterol demethylase, decreases ergosterol synthesis, inhibits fungal cell wall formation. b) Common to azoles: hepatotoxic, QTc prolongation. Unique to posaconazole: GI upset, headaches, thrombophlebitis (60% with peripheral IV), interference with steroid synthesis pathway causing adrenal insufficiency (rare), pseudohyperaldosteronism. c) Oral suspension (requires acidic carbonated beverage, reduced absorption with gastric acid suppression); Oral extended-release tablet (less affected by food/pH, once daily); IV solution.

questions.question: Interactions of tacrolimus with: Ciprofloxacin, Voriconazole, Rifampin, Clarithromycin.

parts.text: Describe the interaction of tacrolimus (a CYP3A4 substrate) with each of the listed drugs.

cohort_answer.text: Tacrolimus is a CYP3A4 substrate. Ciprofloxacin - weakly inhibits CYP3A4, may increase tacrolimus. Voriconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus levels (strongest contraindication; rifabutin should be used instead of rifampin to avoid interaction and reduce risk of acute graft rejection). Clarithromycin (and other macrolides) - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreases tacrolimus. Clarithromycin - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Fluconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increases tacrolimus. Gentamicin + tacrolimus: no true drug-drug interaction, but both can cause nephrotoxicity. MMF + TMP/SMX: no true DDI, both can cause myelosuppression.

cohort_answer.text: Empiric therapy: Liposomal amphoB (3-5mg/kg) +/- flucytosine; High dose echinocandin. Urgent surgery indications: Fungal endocarditis; Severe heart failure with valve dysfunction; Large mobile vegetation with evidence of embolic phenomena. If not a surgical candidate: Step down therapy to fluconazole 400-800mg daily if susceptible isolates, clinical stability, and cleared bloodstream Candida; for patients who cannot undergo valve replacement, long term suppression with fluconazole 400-800mg daily if isolate susceptible; even with surgery, reasonable to consider lifelong prophylaxis due to recurrence risk

parts.text: I choose _______ because of better renal penetration
I choose _______ because I need a drug to cover for bacterial meningitis
I choose _______ because my patient has G6PD
I choose _______ because my patient is on carbamazepine
I choose _______ because it is not a drug that treats C. difficile and it is a drug that has not been strongly associated with causing C. difficile
I choose _______ because it has better activity for CMV

questions.model_answer:
a) Better renal penetration: Cefazolin over cloxacillin (cefazolin achieves high urinary concentrations; cloxacillin is highly protein-bound with poor urinary penetration).
b) Cover bacterial meningitis: Ampicillin over cloxacillin (ampicillin covers Listeria monocytogenes and achieves adequate CSF penetration; cloxacillin does not cover Listeria and penetrates the CNS poorly).
c) Patient has G6PD deficiency: Atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency).
d) Patient on carbamazepine: Fluconazole over caspofungin (carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces caspofungin exposure, requiring dose adjustment; fluconazole avoids this interaction).
e) Not a drug that treats C. difficile and not strongly associated with causing C. difficile: Doxycycline over TMP-SMX (doxycycline carries one of the lowest C. difficile risks among commonly used antibiotics and does not treat CDI).
f) Better activity for CMV: Valganciclovir over valacyclovir (valganciclovir is a ganciclovir prodrug with potent CMV activity; valacyclovir has only modest/prophylactic CMV activity and is primarily an HSV/VZV agent).

questions.question: Antifungal question

parts.text: What component of the cell-wall do azoles inhibit synthesis of?
Which antifungal agent is Pichia kudriavzevii (formerly Candida krusei) intrinsically resistant to?
A patient is infected with Candida auris. They have had no prior exposure to antifungal agents. What class of antifungals would you use empirically?
Name THREE antifungals active in the treatment of mucormycosis.

questions.model_answer:
a) Azoles inhibit synthesis of ergosterol, a key component of the fungal cell membrane (not the cell wall) - by blocking lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase.
b) Pichia kudriavzevii (Candida krusei) is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole.
c) For Candida auris with no prior antifungal exposure, empiric therapy with an echinocandin (e.g., micafungin or caspofungin) is recommended, given the high prevalence of fluconazole resistance in this species.
d) Antifungals active against mucormycosis: liposomal amphotericin B, posaconazole, and isavuconazole.

parts.text: Match the drug-pair choices to the appropriate clinical scenario phrases

questions.model_answer: No specific clinical-scenario phrases were provided in this batch to match against the drug-pair list, so a specific matched answer cannot be given reliably. General rationale for each pair, for reference: Valganciclovir over valacyclovir/acyclovir - superior CMV activity. Famciclovir over acyclovir - once/twice-daily dosing, better bioavailability, similar HSV/VZV coverage. Atovaquone over dapsone - avoids hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Doxycycline over TMP-SMX - avoided in sulfa allergy, low C. difficile risk. Fluconazole over caspofungin - oral bioavailability/step-down therapy for susceptible Candida, but avoided with strong CYP3A4 interactions (e.g., carbamazepine). Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate - reduced nephrotoxicity/infusion reactions. Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem - carbapenem-sparing for susceptible organisms. Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin - better CNS penetration and anaerobic coverage. Metronidazole over clindamycin - lower C. difficile risk. Azithromycin over clarithromycin - fewer CYP3A4 drug interactions (e.g., in a patient on carbamazepine or other CYP3A4 substrates). Ampicillin over cloxacillin - preferred for Enterococcus. Cefazolin over cloxacillin - better tolerability/renal penetration for MSSA bacteremia.
